reader.title: Threatened lynching of Duncan on a Missouri, Kansas and Texas train
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: The only report describes a seized man taken off a train amid yells of "lynch him" with his fate unknown, a threatened lynching with no reported killing and no stated racial element (A1).

A1 reports only that Duncan was tied by passengers and taken off the train amid yells of "lynch him" and that his fate was not known; no killing, no group action beyond the seizure, and no follow-up is reported (A1).
One Dallas dispatch printed in the Memphis Public Ledger is the only report found; no second account or follow-up appeared (A1).

summary.text: The threatened lynching of Duncan took place on the night of March 4, 1881, after a man of that name, described as a Kentuckian, was accused of shooting two men dead on a Missouri, Kansas and Texas passenger train north of Denison.
Passengers tied him and took him off the train at the next station amid cries to lynch him, and his fate was not known when the news was sent out.
The episode is known from a single Dallas dispatch, which gives no race for anyone involved.
According to a Dallas dispatch dated March 5, Duncan was riding the passenger train "en route to Texas" when he "sprang from his seat and shot two men dead without the least provocation."
The dispatch identified one of the dead men as an Indianian and the other as a Tennesseean, but gave neither name.
It did not name the place of the shooting beyond "some point" on the road north of Denison.
The passengers then bound Duncan with a rope.
When the train reached the first station, he was taken off "amid yells of 'lynch him, lynch him,'" though the dispatch did not say who took him or who was yelling.
The dispatch closed with the line "Duncan's fate is not known."
No later report of a lynching, an arrest, an inquest into the two deaths, or a trial appears in the coverage.
The Memphis Public Ledger printed the Dallas dispatch on March 8, 1881, as a brief wire item on its second page.
The item identified the men involved only by home state, called the shooting unprovoked, and reported the cries to lynch without comment.
No other paper's report of the shooting or of Duncan's fate appears in the coverage.

framing.detail: The Public Ledger ran the Dallas dispatch without a headline of its own in the text or editorial comment, calling the shooting one "without the least provocation".
